oneLineAnswer: A prescription tablet for a type of leukemia called Ph+ CML; it blocks the BCR-ABL enzyme driving it.
whatItIs: Bosutinib is a kinase inhibitor. A kinase is an enzyme that can push cells to grow, and blocking one can slow a cancer. Bosutinib is a small molecule that comes as a tablet you swallow. It is sold under the brand name Bosulif and as generic bosutinib tablets. Its chemical formula is C26H29Cl2N5O3, and its molecular weight is about 530.
whatItDoes: Bosutinib blocks BCR-ABL, an abnormal enzyme that drives chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).
It also blocks Src-family enzymes, so it is described as a dual kinase inhibitor.
It is approved for adults with Philadelphia chromosome-positive CML, in chronic, accelerated or blast phase.
It did not block two resistant forms of BCR-ABL called T315I and V299L.
Researchers have tested it in other cancers too, including a phase 2 trial in recurrent glioblastoma.
howPeopleUseIt: It is a tablet. The label says to swallow it whole, once a day with food.
The label tells people to keep taking it until the leukemia gets worse or side effects become intolerable.
The label tells patients not to change or stop their dose unless their doctor says so.
Doctors may add antidiarrheal or anti-nausea medicines, plus fluids, to manage side effects.
It has been studied both as a first leukemia treatment and after other drugs stopped working.

commonSideEffects: Diarrhea is the most common side effect. In one study of 814 adults it affected 80% of them.
Other common effects include nausea, vomiting, belly pain, rash, tiredness, headache and fever.
Blood tests often show low blood cell counts and raised liver enzymes.
In one study of 546 adults, diarrhea usually started about two days in and lasted about two days per episode.
Sixty percent of people in that study had a rise in either ALT or AST, two liver enzymes.
seriousSigns: The label warns bosutinib can cause heart failure, weakened heart pumping and reduced blood flow to the heart.
Fluid can collect around the lungs or heart, or in the legs and feet, causing swelling and breathlessness.
Liver damage is possible. In trials, 2 of 1,711 people had a pattern consistent with drug-induced liver injury.
Low blood counts can lead to infections, bleeding and easy bruising.
Kidney function can fall during treatment, so kidney tests are part of monitoring.
Rare reports after approval include thrombotic microangiopathy and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have happened.
The label lists jaundice, shortness of breath, weight gain, swelling, fever and unusual bleeding as symptoms people should report.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone who has had an allergic reaction to bosutinib, including anaphylaxis, should not take it.
It can harm a fetus, and there is no human pregnancy data to measure that risk.
The label advises women not to breastfeed during treatment.
People taking strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitors, or strong CYP3A inducers, should avoid combining them with bosutinib.
Proton pump inhibitors lower how much bosutinib the body absorbs. The label suggests short-acting antacids or H2 blockers instead.
LiverTox adds that other medicines which can harm the liver should be avoided.

interactions: Bosutinib is broken down by a liver enzyme called CYP3A4.
Strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitors can raise bosutinib levels in the blood and increase side effects.
Strong CYP3A inducers can lower bosutinib levels and may make it work less well.
Proton pump inhibitors reduce absorption, so the label recommends a different kind of acid reducer.
The label advises spacing short-acting antacids or H2 blockers apart from the bosutinib tablet.
pregnancyAndChildren: Bosutinib can harm a fetus. Animal studies found structural abnormalities, pregnancy loss and slowed growth. There are no human pregnancy data, so the human risk is not measured. The label advises a pregnancy test before treatment. It also advises effective contraception during treatment and for two weeks after the last dose. Women are advised not to breastfeed. The generic tablet label carries no pediatric information, pointing instead to the brand product where that information is approved. The label states that safety and effectiveness are not established for children under one year. The same applies to children with accelerated or blast phase disease.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Nobody has measured bosutinib's risk in human pregnancy. Animal studies are the only evidence so far.
The label notes that postmarketing reports are voluntary, so their frequency cannot be reliably estimated.
Effects on fertility in people have not been studied, though animal studies suggest they are possible.
LiverTox says how often bosutinib causes obvious liver injury, and what that injury looks like, is not well defined.
The generic tablet label leaves out pediatric information because of marketing exclusivity on the brand product.

gaps: NCCIH has no bosutinib page. The URL https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/bosutinib returned HTTP 404, so no NCCIH content is cited.

LiverTox on the NCBI Bookshelf blocked automated access with a reCAPTCHA, so the readable copy came from an Internet Archive snapshot taken 2025-02-02 of a page last updated 2017-09-30. That LiverTox text may lag newer label changes.

openFDA and DailyMed host the same manufacturer-authored label text, so label-based claims there are not fully independent of each other. LiverTox, PubChem and ClinicalTrials.gov are separate sources.
No source was found covering human pregnancy outcomes, transfer of bosutinib into breast milk, fertility effects in people, or pediatric use details for the generic product.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were deliberately not fetched or cited because NLM states that content is copyrighted American Society of Health-System Pharmacists material.
summary: This record covers what bosutinib is, how it blocks BCR-ABL in Philadelphia chromosome-positive CML, its label-recorded side effects, interactions and liver risk, plus the pregnancy, breastfeeding and pediatric cautions.
